Perhaps, Mr. Speaker, the same cannot be said of a subject about which there is need for me to speak now at greater length, and I apologize in advance for the length of time that will be required to deal with it. It is, among other things, the discharge of a commitment I made earlier and which I regret I have not been able to discharge before now. I refer to magazines, on which there is an uncertainty that needs to be ended.
The last Liberal administration attempted to act for the preservation of Canadian magazines. The measure which it introduced to that end was perhaps not a perfect one, but it was something. The government which took its place repealed that measure and two years later appointed a royal commission to deal with the same problem. This royal commission was told to work very fast, and it did. The commission reported in May, 1961, but nothing has been done since that time. In the meantime the economic position of Canadian magazines has continued to deteriorate. The uncertainty which has prevailed has itself been harmful to the Canadian periodical press because of its effect upon advertising programs, which are customarily prepared and planned many months in advance of publication. A clear statement of government intentions is therefore necessary in order to dispel uncertainty and permit the industry to base its plans on a clearly defined policy in so far as government action, or lack of action, makes that possible.
The royal commission to which I have referred, which is sometimes called the O'Leary commission, reached the conclusion that a genuinely Canadian periodical press can only exist if Canadian publications are assured of most of the magazine advertising that is directed to Canadians. The commission's two principal recommendations were, first, that a taxpayer should not be allowed to deduct from his income, for tax purposes, expenditures incurred for advertising directed at the Canadian market in a foreign periodical; and second, that the entry into Canada from
58	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Pearson abroad of any periodical containing Canadian domestic advertising should be prohibited under the Customs Tariff.
The government recognizes that the financial problems of Canadian magazines are not due only to the attraction of Canadian advertising by non-Canadian periodicals. There are other causes, including of course the competition of television advertising. Nevertheless, the government accepts the view that in order to survive-and I think the necessity for such survival is admitted, if it can possibly be brought about-Canadian publications must be assured of a reasonable share of the magazine advertising that is directed to Canadian readers.
The importance of maintaining a periodical press as one of the essential means of Canadian self expression hardly needs to be reiterated in this house. That importance was stressed by the royal commission on national development in the arts, letters and sciences as well as the royal commission on publications to which I have referred. It has been recognized by many people in and out of parliament. I am confident, therefore, that there will be support for the legislative action which we now propose.
That action is as follows. First, the Income Tax Act will be amended so as not to allow a taxpayer to deduct from his income, for tax purposes, expenditures after December 31, 1964, for advertising specifically directed at the Canadian market in nonCanadian periodicals. Non-Canadian periodicals will be defined so as to include any future special Canadian editions of foreign periodicals not in existence today. Canadian advertisers in Canadian editions which already exist, for example Time and Reader's Digest, will continue to be allowed to deduct their expenditures for advertising in those periodicals. In making this exception we are taking into account the fact that these special editions have been established in Canada for some years and have made a place for themselves with Canadian readers. This was also recognized in the resolution which the then minister of finance put forward just before the dissolution of the last parliament.
Second, schedule C of the Customs Tariff will be amended to prohibit the entry into Canada of split runs or regional editions containing advertising specifically directed at the Canadian market, and of other magazines, including trade papers, if more than 5 per cent of their advertising space is specifically directed at the Canadian market. I should emphasize that although this proposal relates to the Customs Tariff, it is not designed as a measure of commercial policy. Magazines generally will continue to enter Canada freely and without payment of any customs duty.


It will be recalled that the royal commission on publications recommended that any magazine containing any Canadian domestic advertising should be denied entry into Canada. The government is of the opinion that this step would be too rigorous. Many foreign magazines are imported into Canada and are widely read by Canadians. Many of these magazines contain a limited number of advertisements directed at Canadian readers. The government does not wish to interfere with the reading habits of the Canadian public, nor with the free flow into Canada of magazines containing a modest amount of advertising directed at Canadians. The point of the 5 per cent provision is to avoid disrupting the normal advertising pattern of genuine foreign magazines coming into Canada on their own merits, while guarding against the possibility of abuse in future.
For the purpose of both these measures a periodical will be defined to mean (a) any publication which appears not more frequently than once a week but not less frequently than four times a year; (b) an annual edition of such a publication; and (c) a weekly newspaper supplement not restricted to one particular newspaper but inserted in several newspapers. Journals of learned societies, universities and other like organizations will not be regarded as periodicals.
The government recognizes, Mr. Speaker, as I am sure the house recognizes, that there is no perfect solution for this magazine problem. We must avoid any measures which would interfere with the free flow of information and opinion. That principle sets strict limits to the possible action in this field. At the same time we cannot permit our Canadian periodical press to disappear if we can prevent that disappearance. I believe that the action the government will propose is a proper balancing of these two essential considerations, and I hope it will be recognized as such.
Before leaving this general subject, Mr. Speaker, there is one other comment I would make. Magazines are not the only media of communication which encounter difficulties more or less unique to Canada. In fact I do not know of any other two countries in the world which have this particular problem of communications relationship. Certain other media are also vulnerable to somewhat similar kinds of competition for the advertising which finances them.
The government has already referred the question of community antenna television, which is one aspect of this problem, to the board of broadcast governors. There are also a number of television stations in the United States close to the Canadian border which solicit advertising in Canada and weaken the

position of the private and public Canadian T.V. stations. Finally, there are some signs that metropolitan newspapers in Canada may before long be in danger of coming under foreign ownership and control. These are difficult and complex issues; I do not know of any issue which is more difficult or more complex. The government is giving them careful examination at the present time, and they deserve very careful examination before any decisions are reached with regard to them. But in the meantime it would be wrong to delay action in respect of magazines, which action is urgently needed, so we are proceeding with the magazine aspect of this problem at this time.
It is natural, Mr. Speaker, to pass from this topic to another measure involving our identity as Canadians. It may be recalled that when in opposition we in this party urged that the Canadian Citizenship Act should be amended to remove the apparent discrimination and anomalies concerning loss of citizenship under part III of the act. As a matter of principle, naturalized citizens should surely have an equality of rights and status with natural born citizens. The amending measure referred to in the throne speech will therefore seek to remove these provisions, which could be construed as discriminatory. In essence, the principle of our law should be, and I hope will be, that a Canadian citizen will not be deprived of that status unless he voluntarily accepts or utilizes the citizenship of another country.
I shall refer next, as part of this balanced and wide-ranging program, to the measures by which we will seek to improve the organizational efficiency of government. The establishment of the treasury board, which was referred to by the right hon. gentleman this afternoon, under the presidency of a separate minister was, I would point out, the central recommendation of the royal commission on government organization, the implementation of which is something very dear to the heart of my right hon. friend. And it should be; he set up the commission, and I believe the commission did a very good and valuable job for the country. We think it is a good recommendation. The growth and complexity of government has made the problems of balancing priorities in expenditures greatly more complex than in the past. It has equally multiplied the importance of good management in the public service, and has increased the obstacles to good management. The new minister, who has had long experience, will give his full attention to these and related problems, and in that setting will be responsible for implementing other recommendations of the royal commission.
The Address-Mr. Pearson
The second major change that we will propose in government organization concerns the use of our land resources, about which I was asked a question this afternoon. No two activities are more important to this country than agriculture and forestry. The problems of agriculture are inevitably diverse. We all recognize-indeed the former minister of agriculture has spoken and still speaks quite eloquently on this subject-that many of the worst problems of low farm income are problems primarily in eastern Canada, and that these ought to have more attention than a single minister has been able to give them.
That is one side of the picture. The great and increasing burden of work properly associated with the Department of Agriculture as now constituted under a single minister. The other side of the picture is a paradox. The forest industry is in some respects the major industry of this country; certainly its contribution to our trade and our economic wellbeing is enormous, and the right hon. gentleman put some figures on the record this afternoon which indicate the extent of that importance. And yet, in the apparatus of federal government, it is a comparatively light portfolio; at least it is lighter than some other portfolios.
The explanation of this paradox-the importance of the forest industry yet the lighter work load of the forestry portfolio-is of course due to the fact that the range of federal action relating to forestry is limited by constitutional considerations. This inevitably limits the role which can be played by even the most able and dedicated minister of forestry. Yet surely it is most important that forestry, which is so vital to our economy, should not be regarded as a minor portfolio. What the government properly can do in this sphere must be well done.
The solution we propose is to match up these different, indeed opposite, problems in agriculture and forestry. We will bring the load on the agriculture portfolio to more reasonable proportions and at the same time increase the importance of the forestry portfolio by combining forestry with an important, a growing and a related aspect of the work of the Department of Agriculture; that is to say, with the work of rural development, and we will have a ministry of forestry and rural development.
I believe, Mr. Speaker, that this reorganization will have three good results. It will mean a better balancing of the work load for ministers and officials and will therefore improve efficiency. Second, it will increase and improve the attention which in the past could be given to certain agricultural matters. Third, it means that forestry will occupy a more important place in the structure of

The Address-Mr. Pearson government and will get the best possible care within the limits of the federal government's constitutional responsibility.
The throne speech also indicated that it is our intention to bring forward further measures to assist in the improvement of farm income and the progress of our agricultural industry. We will be dealing with the details of this on another occasion, but I may indicate now that we hope to broaden and expand substantially the scale of farm credit. We expect also to be able to undertake a major improvement in crop insurance which we have been discussing with the provinces, and also to introduce measures to meet the problem of the cost of farm machinery.

I should like now, Mr. Speaker, to say a few words about the state of the economy, and fewer words about the prospects for the forthcoming year. In recent years in Canada we have not had the vigorous economy that our people need in order to maintain the employment which is desirable. Without wishing now to give any suggestion of complacency about our economic situation, it is gratifying to be able to say that it is better, that prospects look more promising, than when we convened for the first session of this parliament. The year 1963 was one of considerable gains in almost all economic sectors. Business operated closer to capacity than it has for years. Industrial production rose appreciably, especially automobile production where the shipments of Canadian made vehicles increased to an all-time high of over 630,000 units or some 23 per cent above the 1962 figures.
The textile industry, which is one of our most important industries, also increased its output and stepped up its sales. Indeed, the production of almost all kinds of goods rose to meet both increasing domestic demand

and to supply our markets abroad. Another very important sector of our economy which registered substantially increased activity in 1963 was the house building industry. This industry plays a major role in creating employment opportunities, particularly during the winter months when seasonal unemployment is at its highest. The number of housing units started last year totalled 148,000 units as compared with some 130,000 in 1962, and the estimated value of residential construction reached a new high of approximately $1,800 million, which was roughly more than $300 million above the previous year. The winter construction incentive bonus, about which some hon. members opposite were sceptical when it was announced, has been an undoubted success and some 32,000 units have already been approved under this program.
We take great pride, and justifiably so, Mr. Speaker, that our country is one of the foremost trading nations of the world. Last year's improvement in Canada's foreign trade is particularly encouraging. Our trade with all countries exceeded $13,500 million and was the highest value ever recorded, according to most recent information. Exports rose by 10 per cent to reach a new high of almost $7 billion. Imports increased by some 5 per cent over 1962, so our commodity trade surplus last year was the largest since 1952. A welcome and very important aspect of this improvement in export trade has been the reduction in total current account deficit. The estimated deficit for 1963 is some $500 million, as compared with $850 million of a deficit a year ago or an average deficit of some $1 billion recorded annually over most of the last 10 years.
Turning now to agriculture-and the right hon. gentleman had something to say about that this afternoon-I may say that Canadian farmers harvested and sold the biggest wheat crop in history. Preliminary reports indicate that farm cash income in 1963 will have reached a record level of over $3 billion. Labour income in 1963 also rose substantially over 1962, while the number of employed increased significantly. The unemployment rate in December, seasonally adjusted, was under 5 per cent, the lowest level in many years.
In short, Mr. Speaker, 1963 was a year of substantial economic achievement by the people of Canada. I do not intend to claim that this achievement, this improvement, was due merely to the efforts of the government. However, I do claim that the measures introduced to date by the government have helped to move the economy forward. Having said this, let me repeat that there is much to be done before we can be satisfied with economic conditions in this country and before we can 20220-5
The Address-Mr. Pearson be confident of steady progress in the future. Unemployment particularly remains one of our most urgent problems. Despite the progress made in 1963, the present level of nearly 5 per cent is still much too high in comparison with a number of other industrially advanced countries, and all our efforts must be directed toward reducing unemployment.
Unemployment is not, as we all know, a simple problem. We have introduced measures, both short and medium term, to improve the situation. We have, amongst other things, provided incentives to attract new industrial facilities and revive economic activity in areas of chronic unemployment. There are still too many such areas in this country. It does not help very much to tell someone unemployed in Cape Breton, where the percentage may be higher than the national average, or in Quebec, that there is no unemployment in some other part of Canada 3,000 miles away. We have recognized these area problems. We have also introduced measures to reduce winter unemployment. We have encouraged the re-employment of older workers. We have increased federal assistance for the training of both employed and unemployed workers. We have established a manpower consultative service to assist employers and unions in effecting manpower adjustments resulting from industrial change. In one way or another, Mr. Speaker, our economy must continue to expand fast enough to take care of our rapidly growing population and to provide for the increasing needs of all sections of the community in all parts of the country.
If we are to continue the reduction of the deficit in our international current account, and that is our objective, we must increase our exports even further, not only of agricultural products and partially manufactured products but also completely manufactured goods. We have therefore welcomed, as I am sure all hon. members of the house have welcomed, the United States trade initiative that has come to be called the "Kennedy round negotiations, and we look forward to our participation in the forthcoming trade and tariff conference to be convened at the beginning of May, under the auspices of GATT, in Geneva, as an excellent opportunity for bringing about a substantial reduction of world trade barriers. Canada has already indicated that it is prepared in any such negotiations to make concessions that match the benefits that may come to us. We are also prepared to play our full part in the United Nations economic conference which will be opening before that in March.
A third problem that exists, and has always existed in Canada, is the differences__
and I have just mentioned this in passing- in the levels of prosperity, income and

The Address-Mr. Pearson employment in different sections of our vast country. In a diverse country like ours there are bound to be such differences. We have, however, taken steps through the area development agency, and other agencies, to stimulate economic activity, in co-operation with provincial jurisdictions, in those areas which have lagged significantly behind the rest of Canada.
This afternoon, Mr. Speaker, there was a reference by the right hon. Leader of the Opposition to another aspect of our economic problems, the rising cost of living and the dangers of inflation. I would like to put the facts in this matter on the record, and in order to remove the impression that we are facing dangers now in excess of those that existed in recent years I think these will be illuminating facts.
In the past nine months from April last year, when we took office, to January this year the index of consumer prices has risen by 1.4 per cent. Of course we regret that increase, but I would point out as a comparison that in the first nine months of the administration of my right hon. friend, from June 1957 to March 1958, the price index rose not by 1.4 per cent but by 2.2 per cent. Of course, Mr. Speaker, having said that I recognize that comparisons over as short a period as nine months can be misleading, so let us take a longer period in order to put this situation in perspective.
The right hon. gentleman was in office for almost six years, two months less than six years, and in that time the consumer price index rose by 8.8 per cent, from June 1957 to April 1963. What had happened in the previous six years less two months, a parallel period, from August 1951 to June 1957? The price index had risen by 5.3 per cent.
I am not saying that this comparison means we have nothing to worry about. Of course we have, and I do not get any particular satisfaction out of showing that we did better in one period of time under a Liberal government in this particular matter than was done in a similar period of time under a Conservative government; but if this is taken as a major danger and a major reflection on the policy of this government, then I think it should be put in perspective.
I would make this point. We all know that it is harder to keep prices stable when the economy is buoyant. The years of the previous government were not years of a buoyant economy. The years before, over which I compared prices, were years that included the Korean war and the 1955-56 boom in this country, and the period since we took office in April last has been a period of the strongest economic activity since 1956. In these

circumstances then we can take some satisfaction, without ignoring the dangers that exist, in the fact that prices under Liberal governments have risen less than when the party opposite was in office.
Looking now at the year ahead, 1964, the latest economic forecasts indicate that economic activity in Canada is expected to continue to expand at about the same rate as in 1963. The preliminary reports suggest that capital expenditures will again rise and consumer expenditures on goods and services should continue to advance as well.
Canada's prospects for the year ahead will also depend to a large extent, as they always do, on world conditions. These conditions seem now to be favourable for sustained growth, especially in the United States, so that we may expect foreign demand for our exports to remain high in the months ahead. This will naturally have a sustaining effect on employment and incomes, and should contribute to the further strengthening of our balance of payments position.
In the months ahead the government will continue, by appropriate measures, to assist our economy in the necessary process of adjustment to new conditions, and to foster an economic climate in which the process of industrial development may be smooth and speedy. I think we can say, without complacency, that the economic activity has now been stimulated to the point where we can proceed to attack the tough and persistent problems of chronic unemployment, of regional economic underdevelopment and of continuing deficits in international payments with better prospects of success than in the last few years.
Until recently the relatively low general level of activity of our national economy greatly reduced the possibility of dealing effectively with these special problems. That deficiency has been remedied, and we can now look forward to making faster progress on the problems of regional development and also, I believe, on the fundamental problems of our payments balance with other countries.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I would like to conclude my remarks by saying something about parliament, its place in our national life, what we might do to improve its procedures and make it more efficient

a matter which was mentioned this afternoon by the right hon. gentleman-and then say a few words, if I may, on the problem of national unity.
As the throne speech indicated, the house will be asked, and I am sure the house will be glad to do this, to agree to the re-establishment of the i committee on procedures and the organization of parliament. I am sure all of us are anxious to see that committee at work again, Mr. Speaker, under your distinguished

chairmanship, so that it can make recommendations for the more effective dispatch of public business.
The complexities of government, and of the issues which we will be discussing and attempting to solve here, are creating problems which the architects of our confederation could not have foreseen. Today there is more scheduling and more organization involved in mail delivery or, if you like, garbage collection in Montreal or Toronto than was needed for the whole country in the days of the fathers of confederation. And in this growing complexity problems no longer occur in simple shapes, compact packages, or predictable rhythms. I believe, sir, that this very complexity, as it is developing in public affairs, is creating inevitably a new approach to politics.
Now this does not mean, nor does it require, the abandonment of party politics. The party system and the parliamentary system are absolutely inseparable, and sparks from the honest and vigorous clash of party opinion in parliament will continue to light beacons showing us the path to reform, toward better government and toward men's betterment. But I believe there is a growing area of parliamentary action, particularly as it affects national purpose, national security and human welfare which, involving all Canadians, transcends partisan or parochial interests. I am convinced that underlying much of the criticism and some of the cynicism about what goes on in parliament is a compelling desire on the part of millions of Canadians to see greater recognition given by politicians to the fact that there are many issues on which all Canadians must unite if a strong and united nation is to survive. Canadian parliaments have often shown in the past that they can agree on important issues and operate quickly and effectively in an emergency. It is my hope, and I am sure it is the hope of all hon. members, that the critics of our conduct will see increasing evidence of this trend in the coming months.
I believe that in re-establishing our committee on procedures and the organization of parliament all of us share a sincere concern that its work will be fruitful. But I should like to see something done now, pending the report of that committee-and the committee work may take some time. I should like to see agreement now, if it could be arranged, on some procedural changes in the interests of greater efficiency.	*
All party leaders spoke at length last October when the motion for the appointment of the select committee was introduced. All of us expressed concern that nothing should diminish the rights of the opposition and of private members. That concern is a

The first is the allocation of time to specific legislation. I realize this is a most important concession for an opposition to make, but I would remind the house that it is a concession which the party I lead was prepared to make in 1962 when in opposition.

speechtext:
I think that could certainly be looked into. I know it is the procedure at Westminster, and perhaps it would be an additional protection for the rights of the opposition. It certainly should be considered in any discussion we would be having on this matter.
I have talked about the economic state of the country, but I should like to add that, as man cannot live by bread alone, a nation's progress must be measured by things other than national product and national income. There are national values that must be strengthened and national unity that must be made secure. All of us here in this house know that there are strains on that unity. There is evidence of this every day before us. These strains are being widely discussed in the context of federal-provincial relations and, increasingly, in the context of confederation itself. I believe some of these strains were eased by the spirit which prevailed in November's federal-provincial meetings. The desire and, indeed, the determination of the ten provincial premiers to work with the federal government in keeping a strong and united nation was reassuring and heartening.
Consultation and co-operation in this federal state of ours is growing as the need for it grows. Since this government took office there have been several important federal-provincial conferences. There have been two meetings of heads of governments-prime minister and premiers-in 1963 up to January, 1964; and there have been four meetings of ministers-ministers dealing with the Canada pension plan, ministers of trade and industry, ministers of agriculture, and ministers of

fisheries. Other main federal-provincial conferences to take place in 1964 include meetings of the ministers of labour in March, a meeting of the prime ministers on March 31, a meeting of the ministers responsible for Indian affairs in May, a meeting of the Minister of Justice with the provincial attorneys general at a constitutional conference, a meeting of ministers responsible for dealing with civil emergency planning, a meeting of the ministers of agriculture, and of trade and industry. Later this year there will be a meeting of forestry ministers and a meeting of the resource ministers council in June. There is also to be a meeting of the federal-provincial committee on the centennial of confederation. There are, in addition, to be numerous meetings throughout the year at the official level in all fields of government activity. Also, to improve this consultation and co-operation, the government is establishing within the privy council office a small unit responsible for general liaison arrangements with the provinces, which will be under my direction.
Hon. members may be aware that in our reorganization of cabinet committees we have established a standing committee on federal-provincial relations, which is also under my chairmanship. But in spite of organization, and indeed in spite of good will, the problems of federation will remain. They are inevitable in our kind of federal government, and they are particularly complicated in a country like Canada.
The foundation on which the problems of our federation must be resolved is acceptance, in the first place, of the full partnership of English speaking and French speaking Canadians. In our national federation each province has its own rights, its own resources and its own jurisdiction. This is particularly significant, surely, in the case of Quebec which, as well as being a province, is also the home of most of our French speaking Canadians, the guardian of their language, their traditions and their way of life. The solution, on the essential foundation which I have mentioned, to ouf problems must be found in what we call co-operative federalism. That means to me that the federal government must of course always seek the approval of provincial governments, when that is necessary under our constitution, before decisions are made. That is obvious. But there must also be consultation on matters which, while within the jurisdiction of the federal government, are shared constitutionally with provincial governments, or are of such great and immediate importance to provincial governments that, for good results, provincial support and co-operation must be obtained.

At the same time the federal government nas obligations to discharge to the people of Canada as a whole. The necessity, which is admitted, of increased consultation with provinces need not and must not interfere with the discharge of those obligations. The issue is not, and must not, become "provincial rights" versus "Canada first". These slogans and any others which represent competing approaches to national unity are dangerous and could be destroying; and they misrepresent the actual position. This is how Professor Corry of Queen's University puts it in an article on "Constitutional trends and federalism":
We are likely to have to live for a long time with the equivocal structure called co-operative federalism. It has arisen because several separate governments share a divided responsibility for regulating a single economic and social structure. It is most unlikely that any constitution could be devised which would enable each to perform its specific functions adequately without impinging seriously on the others. So their activities are inevitably mingled, and co-operative arrangements must be worked out. In the result, formal powers are not co-terminous with operating responsibilities; the two levels of government as well as the several state and provincial governments interpenetrate one another in many places and ways. Under the heat and pressure generated by social and economic change in the twentieth century, the distinct strata of the older federalism have begun to melt and flow into one another.

This is only one reason why any government in Ottawa must confront forces which would separate or divide us, with the aspirations of all Canadians and the determination of the vast majority of them in every part and province of our country to remain Canadian citizens; citizens of no mean country; citizens of a nation which is greater than the sum of its parts. The dream of a strong and united Canada, as we all know, is older than confederation itself. Indeed, it motivated confederation. It was in the mind of an hon. member of this house, Louis Honore Frechette, in 1875 when he made this statement:
We will form but one great nation with deep-rooted patriotism and noble aspirations, working as one to common prosperity, and advancing together towards a great and productive future.
Mr. Speaker, on this ideal alone can we find the solution to the problem of the relations between English speaking and French speaking Canadians. It is a problem which by its very nature is highly emotional and particularly sensitive to gusts of passion and prejudice. There is no easy, magic solution to it. Diatribes in either of our languages will contribute nothing to national unity but much to national disunity. No magic will
The Address-Mr. Pearson dissolve hostilities which are engendered by extremism on either side. No magic will educate the suspicious, satisfy the legitimate aspirations of Quebec, remove understandable anxieties outside Quebec; in short, make the problem go away. Moreover, the problem is complicated by loose talk and misunderstanding about the meaning of such words as "biculturalism" and "bilingualism".

What do we mean by biculturalism? Not, surely, that our nation has or will have only two cultural sources, French and English, each exclusive of the other. For one thing, English culture and French culture are not, and cannot be, separate and distinct from each other or from other cultural strains in Canada. Above all, biculturalism does not mean that these other cultural strains in our society, non Anglo-Saxon or non-French, should be discouraged from making their own strong and enriching contribution to what we are trying to develop in Canada.
Cultural segregation, or cultural separatism, is no more welcome than some other forms of segregation or separatism. Equally to be rejected would be any attempt at cultural absorption by social or political pressure. This is especially the case when the political foundation of a federal state is based on two language groups, with a consequent emphasis on duality which might seem to depreciate the cultural importance of other racial groups in our population. Bicultural does not, as I understand it, and must never mean this kind of exclusiveness, with any assumption or appearance of superiority. What biculturalism in our country does and should mean is that there are two strains, French and, for want of a better word, English, which were the foundation of our national society.

speechtext: Hear, hear.

There must be no pressure on one to absorb the other, but they should develop alongside each other; each, I hope, influencing and improving the other and each influenced and enriched by the cultural contribution of other racial groups and strains which are to be encouraged.
Similarly with bilingualism. Surely it must not be given a restrictive or coercive meaning. It does not mean, as I see it, that every Canadian will be forced to learn two official languages, or that the two official languages, English and French, must be used in every part of Canada in official texts and public declarations. That would be impracticable and unnecessary, and in any event is a matter for the provinces to decide. The federal government, however, has an obligation in this linguistic field to ensure that the rights

The Address-Mr. Pearson of the French language, as guaranteed in our constitution, are preserved and can be exercised; an obligation to ensure that a Canadian using French in federal offices and in respect of federal activities and services will not be discouraged from such use or made to feel a foreigner, especially in his own capital, by another Canadian refusing to acknowledge his right to use the French tongue. Eventually, I believe it must become normal and accepted for all federal services to use both languages interchangeably wherever there are Canadians of both languages living and working.
1 also hope that eventually in dual language regions and communities the provincial educational systems would be able to give all children the opportunity to become fluent in both languages. Surely this should be considered as a privilege, as a positive asset, rather than as a burden. We are a very fortunate people in Canada in that our two official languages are two of the world's greatest universal tongues, English and French. We should be proud to make the most of that privilege.
I repeat, however, that this evolution toward genuine bilingualism which is taking place should not be forced or coercive. It should recognize that there are parts of Canada where French is not spoken at all because the French speaking population is nonexistent or almost non-existent in those areas. A department of education is likely to take a very different attitude to bilingualism in such a part of Canada than one where each language group is strongly represented. Furthermore, even in the civil service, where the federal government has a direct obligation, the long overdue move to real and accepted bilingualism must not, in my view, be made in such a way as to create a feeling of injustice among those in the civil service who are now unilingual and were known to be so when employed. It would be wrong and unfair to penalize such persons now. Efficiency and experience must be the overriding factors in advancement in the federal services. But policies should be adopted so that in the future a third factor, bilingualism, will become normal because unilingualism will be the exception rather than the rule.
There is one thing more on this subject I should like to say. Because we recognize two official languages and must make that recognition a reality in practice wherever that is necessary and desirable, this does not mean that the same official recognition should be extended to any other languages. Such languages can, and I believe should, be used and studied and kept alive in a cultural

sense. But we have only two official languages which require official sanction for Canada as a whole.
Surely, Mr. Speaker, it is the responsibility of all hon. members of this house to overcome rather than create misunderstandings at this time, to avoid rather than engender resentments, and to repair rather than tear. This, it seems to me, is the only possible attitude for honourable men who really believe in Canada and Canada's future as a great nation. All of us here are called upon to present the case against prejudice, against dissension, against extremism at every opportunity, and beyond this place across Canada from the Atlantic to the Pacific.
I know that every hon. member of the house, to whatever party he belongs, believes sincerely in that. I know every hon. member of the house feels in his heart that we will not be unworthy of our forefathers as we face this problem. I refuse to believe, as I know you refuse to believe, that we cannot rise to the occasion, match our problems and be equal to our opportunities. I refuse to believe that when the crying need is for unity in the world, for peace and security for all men, for the growing recognition of the realities and rewards of interdependence, with men in all continents coming together or being driven together, we in this country must move apart.
On a Canadian grave in France there is an epitaph which I believe captures what all of us in this house seek. It is on the headstone over the grave of a Canadian boy who won the Victoria Cross and who was buried in the first of far too many war cemeteries. Whether he was English speaking or French speaking I do not know; some of both races lie in all those cemeteries side by side. The epitaph on the grave of this particular young V.C. boy, which was chosen by his Canadian mother, reads:
How blessed it is for brethren to dwell together in unity.
It is for us, sir, to seek that unity too.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure that members in all parts of the house have listened with keen interest to the two very excellent speeches made today by the Leader of the Opposition and the Prime Minister. I think all hon. members will agree when I say that the passionate and eloquent appeal of the Prime Minister for unity, understanding and mutual good will will find a ready response in the hearts of the members of the house and in the hearts of people in all parts of Canada. I was interested this afternoon when the right hon. Leader of the Opposition mentioned that Caligula had once appointed his

horse to the cabinet. It occurred to me there had been prime ministers who had done that for part of a horse on many occasions.
One of the things that has impressed me most about the speech from the throne is its colossal failure to say anything about the problem of insufficient economic growth and unemployment. On the first page there is this one sentence:
My government will attempt to make its full contribution... to fostering the full employment of our people and the efficient growth of our economy.
There is nothing mentioned about what the government intends to do, no stirring program set out as to what the government is going to undertake to combat unemployment. When the Prime Minister assumed his present office he said to the people of Canada in a national broadcast that this was "a time to excite the daring and test the strong". Certainly, Mr. Speaker, I can find nothing exciting in this very pallid phrase to indicate that the government is going, as it says, to make its full contribution to fostering the full employment of our people and the efficient growth of our economy.
Instead of outlining a bold and imaginative program the Prime Minister has told us with some pride, and justifiably so, that the economy has improved during the past year. This is quite right. Increased exports and fortuitous sales of wheat to China and the Soviet union have given our economy a shot in the arm with the result that this has improved our balance of payments position and has reduced slightly the total number of unemployed.
I would submit, Mr. Speaker, that there are two factors which we must not overlook. The first is that this economic growth has been erratic and promises to be sporadic. In the three years prior to 1962 our economy was virtually at a standstill. In 1962 the gross national product, in real terms, rose by 6 per cent. All the figures are not in for 1963, but the latest estimate is that the gross national product in 1963 will have grown by 4J per cent. The national industrial conference board, as reported in the Financial Post, estimates that in this year 1964 the gross national product in real terms will rise 3.1 per cent. My own feeling is that this is too low an estimate, and I think it will be higher. But the important thing to realize is that there is nothing in the speech from the throne and nothing in any action taken by the government that will introduce fundamental policies to provide for a steady and sustained economic growth and full employment.
The other thing we have to keep in mind is that unemployment has not dropped correspondingly with any increase in economic
The Address-Mr. Douglas activity. We find that in 1961 the average unemployment throughout the year was 7.2 per cent of the labour force. In 1962 this had dropped to 6 per cent and in 1963 the average for the year was 5.6 per cent. At mid-January of this year there were 466,000 unemployed, or 7 per cent of the labour force. But this was not distributed very evenly. It consisted of 9.1 per cent of the labour force in Quebec and 12.6 per cent of the labour force in the Atlantic provinces. I submit, Mr. Speaker, that an economy in which on the national average one person in 15 is walking the streets, and in Quebec almost one person in ten and in the Atlantic provinces one person in eight is out of a job, is an economy that ought to give us some concern.
I suggest that the government has never really come to grips with the root of the problem of insufficient economic growth and unemployment. We have been poking around at the edge of it. We have not even got close to the root causes. We in this party suggest that the problem does not lie primarily in production. We have in Canada idle men, idle plants, idle resources. Our major problem is the inability of large sections of our population to purchase the goods which our economy is capable of producing.
One of the outstanding economists in the world, certainly one of the best on this continent, is Leon Keyserling, who was one of Roosevelt's young braintrusters and was later chairman of the economic advisory council to President Truman. Just recently he has written an article in "New University Thought", and I want to quote some of the things he says because they constitute a keen analysis of our North American economy. He said this:
We don't have a production problem In the United States: we have a distribution problem. We will never make any sizeable progress against the unemployment problem.. .unless we recognize that the reason for the unemployment problem, the cause of the unemployment problem, is the bad distribution of income.
He goes on to point out that in the United States there are 38 million people living in a state of poverty and another 39 million people living in a state of deprivation, or two fifths of the population of the United States who are living below a decent standard of living.
If we take the trouble to look at Canada we will see that there is some similarity. The latest year for which income tax figures are available is 1961. We find that in that year the total labour force was 6,518,000, and that of that number more than two million or about 30 per cent did not earn enough to pay income tax. Of the 4J million who are left, the top 25 per cent received nearly 45 per cent of the total income after paying

The Address-Mr. Douglas their taxes and the bottom 25 per cent of the income taxpayers received less than 12 per cent of the total income after they had paid their taxes.
Fifty five per cent of the income taxpayers did not earn $4,000 a year, and 34 per cent did not earn $3,000 a year. Thirty four per cent of the 44 million is roughly li million. If you add to that the two million who did not pay income tax at all, if you add their wives and children, if you add the unemployed, the old age pensioners who have very little other income beside their pensions, widows and their children, the small farmers and the fishermen whose incomes are low, it is probably not too large an estimate to say that there are between seven million and eight million people in Canada who are living either on or below the borderline of poverty. Two fifths of the nation is living below a decent subsistence level.
We in this party say that the time has come for the government to mount a massive assault, and make a declaration of war against poverty. In such a war we will find that our economic interests and our humanitarian instincts coincide, because any war on poverty will turn out not only to be good economics but also to be good social ethics. If I may quote Keyserling again, he says in his article that "the best kind of attack on poverty is full employment and economic growth. The only way to get full employment and high economic growth is to make a massive attack on poverty. There is no distinction between the two problems."
It is interesting to note that President Johnson in his state of union message to congress said this:
This administration, here and now, declares unconditional war on poverty in America.
Last week, speaking in New York, President Johnson said that "A nation that cannot care for the many who are poor will not have the strength to care for the few who are rich."
We are not suggesting a share the wealth program. What we are suggesting is a distribution of our idle capacity to meet the needs of a large segment of our population who live in fear and insecurity. Professor Keyserling suggests that in the United States there is idle potential capacity of between $60 billion and $75 billion. Estimates have been made by economists in this country that the potential here is between $4 billion and $7 billion. We submit that to put idle people to work in idle plants and on idle resources with a potential production of between $4 billion and $7 billion a year in goods and

services would adequately provide for enlarged educational institutions, for the building of hospitals, for getting rid of slums, building good homes, urban renewal, and the things that this country needs. You can have not only poverty of individuals but communities can have social poverty, they can have collective poverty. We need to make an assault on poverty within our entire country.
I should like to suggest briefly the five things we have advocated in our program as being the best way to wage war on poverty in Canada:
1.	To improve our social security measures. Keyserling said in his article that we need to direct a larger part of our national income to those who consume. Social security measures are not only humanitarian, they not only consist of trying to be our brother's keeper, but in economic terms they are important because they redistribute income and help to maintain purchasing power. They therefore help to maintain full employment.
2.	Higher wages. We do not believe that wages should grow faster than productivity. In recent years, for most industries, wages have lagged behind productive gains. When people speak of wage increases being disastrous they fail to recognize that unless there are increased wages there cannot be increased consumption.
3.	We say we ought to have higher incomes for small farmers and fishermen and such self employed people whose incomes are inadequate.
4.	We think there ought to be the right kind of tax reductions. Tax reductions aimed at the rich who do not need them will not increase the consumption of consumer goods. If we are to have tax reductions, they ought to be tax reductions for the low and middle income groups who will use this additional money in order to purchase consumer goods.
5.	We say that one of the best ways to wage war on poverty is by a massive public spending program to provide schools, technical institutes, university facilities, and to provide the retraining which is necessary for easing the pressure of structural unemployment.
It is known by every member of this house, Mr. Speaker, that Canada faces an educational crisis; that we are competing in a world in which scientific training, research and technical know-how are important if this country is to survive. According to the last available figures, out of every 100 children who started in grade 1 only 14 got to the last year in high school, and fewer than five got to the last year in university. No country can really be great in this scientific age unless it

trains more scientists, more research people, more engineers, more architects, more doctors, more nurses and more teachers, in order to fit more of our people to take their place in a highly automated society in this era of cybernation.
We are told by the best educational authorities that in the next three decades we shall have to double or treble our university and high school facilities. Unless we do this we will fall behind into the backwaters of the world. We shall obtain, by making war on poverty, by massive public spending, the increase in our educational facilities necessary to harness the scientific revolution for the purpose of increasing production, raising living standards, providing social security, and giving to our people a chance to enjoy the good life.
I know, of course, that someone is going to immediately say, if you talk about spending where are you going to get the money to do this spending? I am sure members have seen the report of the O.E.C.D., the organization for economic co-operation and development. I should like to quote from the Globe and Mail for February 7, and the date line is Ottawa. The article reads in part as follows:
Although the business tempo has stepped up in recent years, the stimulus of higher budget deficits may be required to bring about full employment in Canada, the organization for economic co-operation and development has suggested following a second look at the Canadian economy.
Farther down the article reads:
The time may come when the Canadian authorities would wish to inject a more direct stimulus to domestic demand.
This is exactly what we are saying, that the problem is to balance consumption with production, not to balance figures in a book. The problem is to balance the economy so that it provides full employment for every ablebodied person so that we provide sufficient demand for the volume of consumer goods which we are capable of producing.
Mr. Speaker, we think that Canada should be launching an all out war against poverty. That is why, when we look at the speech from the throne, we are a little disappointed that it has nothing to say about this very important matter.
Yesterday the seconder of the motion, the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard said I had been telling people for 25 years that the Liberal party was not a genuinely progressive party, and he refuted my statement by saying "Look at the speech from the throne; it is bringing down a labour code with a minimum wage and with some minimum provisions to protect the workers who come under federal jurisdiction". Mr. Speaker, the pledge to give the workers of Canada a national labour code was made by the Liberal party in its 20220-6
The Address-Mr. Douglas convention of 1919, 45 years ago; and now, when it looks like it is going to deliver what it promised after 45 years, the hon. member wants me to crown its members with a laurel wreath for finally getting around to it. As a matter of fact I strongly suspect that if the government were not in a minority position we might not even be getting this, 45 years later.
I want to know where is the government's program for economic recovery. One of the things that was promised in the election last year was the Canada development corporation. It was described by the Minister of Finance as the keystone in the Liberal program for economic recovery. I have the Liberal program here, and this is what it said the Canadian development corporation was for:
To finance new enterprises in Canada; to increase Canadian production and to reverse the trend toward absentee ownership of Canadian industry.
Where is it? The minister introduced it and put it on the order paper last session. Now it has been dropped. Yesterday the minister said they were' going to wait for the royal commission to report. Why did he put it on the order paper last year if he was going to wait for the commission's report? As the Financial Post said a short time ago, and I am inclined to think it right, the investment companies of this country were putting pressure on the minister with the result it is to be discarded or so badly emasculated that its own mother won't recognize it. This great keystone of economic recovery has now gone into the discard.
Then there is the Canada pension plan. Mr. Speaker, we have had three Canada pension plans. First of all we had the plan presented to the people of Canada by the Secretary of State for External Affairs on behalf of the Liberal party on January 30, 1962. It was a program in which participants were to pay one half of 1 per cent of their income up to $6,000, both by the employer and the employee, and the contributory pension was to be $167 a month at age 70 after they had paid for at least 10 years.
Then on July 18 last year the Minister of National Health and Welfare brought down a plan providing for a 1 per cent contribution by employer and employee. The earnings-related benefits were to constitute 30 per cent of the amount paid up to a maximum $4,000, and at age 70 the maximum pension after contributing for 10 years would be $100 per month.
Now, on January 11, 1964 we got the third version announced by the Prime Minister, and the earnings-related benefits have been cut from 30 per cent down to 20 per cent and at age 70, providing a man has paid for 10 years or more, the maximum contributory

The Address-Mr. Douglas pension will be $75 per month. So we have gone from $167 a month to $100 a month down to $75 a month.
I want to point out that there is no excuse for cutting the benefits. The government will get more money now, under its present proposal, than under the proposal it made last July. First of all, the proposal of last July suggested that the $10 increase in old age security pension was going to come out of this fund, but now it is going to be paid out of an increase in the old age security tax. Also, the 1 per cent premium was to be on $4,000. Now it is going to be on $4,500. Therefore this plan will have more money coming into it than would have come into the plan submitted on July 18 last, yet the benefits are going to be cut and, as the Prime Minister said in writing to the provincial premiers, the cost of the plan will be reduced by at least one fifth.
Why has this change been made? We know there has been a lobby by the insurance companies, led by Mr. Kilgour, who has said "Let's raise a storm." We have seen the storm, but it has been mostly wind. We have heard the protests of the premier of Ontario, who seems to have offered himself as the spokesman for the insurance companies; but what disappoints us most is the Prime Minister's statement to the provinces when in his memorandum to the premiers he said this:
Some provincial governments have, however, put forward the view that a pension of $175 for a single person at age 70, or of $250 for a married couple at 70, in a plan with a 10 year maturity period, might incline some people to withdraw from private pension plans.
To meet this concern, the federal government is prepared to propose that the eamings-related pensions be reduced from 30 to 20 per cent of pensionable earnings.
Well, Mr. Speaker, all I want to say to the Prime Minister is that cutting the eamings-related benefits to please Premier Robarts and to please the insurance companies has not done any good at all. In spite of this appeasement they still object to the plan. I hope the Prime Minister will revert to the plan of July 18 last, put it on the statute books, and let the premier of Ontario accept the responsibility for taking the people of Ontario out of a plan that will give better benefits for the money paid than any provincial or any private plan can do. What I am saying is that I hope the Prime Minister will adopt the slogan of Admiral Dewey, "Full speed ahead and damn the torpedoes."
Mr. Speaker, I now want to mention another item and, if I may, move an amendment. The third item that I am disappointed to see missing from the throne speech is any mention of medicare. The Liberal party's program is a very interesting document, and it promised a medicare program that would-

-cover costs of doctors' and diagnostic services in the office, home or hospital by general practitioners, surgeons and specialists.
It goes on to say that these services will be free for children up to the time they leave school and for people over 65, and for other Canadians will cover doctors' bills above $25 per year per person.
There is a growing feeling across Canada that private plans, doctor sponsored plans and insurance company sponsored plans, cannot meet the health needs of the Canadian people. These plans have rendered a great service in the past, but they have now come to the point where the amount they must charge per family is so high that a great many of the middle income and low income groups just cannot stay in them, so that more and more people are left out; and the more people are left out, naturally the cost for those who remain in goes up. The time has come when the government, in co-operation with the provinces, has to step into the field of medicare and do in the field of medical and surgical care exactly what the governments have already done in the field of hospital care.
I therefore move, seconded by my hon. friend from Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge):
That the following words be added to the amendment immediately at the end thereof:
This house also regrets that Your Excellency's advisers have failed to make provision for federal participation, in co-operation with the provinces, in a government sponsored and government operated medicare program for all Canadians.
There are some other things which are missing from this speech from the throne. There is no mention of raising the age limit for family allowances to 18 years where children are still attending school. There is no mention of the two price system for wheat, which was to give a measure of stability to prairie farmers and which was promised by the government on several occasions during the last election.
Before I sit down I should like to say a few words with reference to international affairs. I should like to express the position which this party has consistently taken, and the position upon which we stand. We believe that the government ought to recognize mainland China. We think we ought to end the farce of trying to pretend that General Chiang Kai-shek represents and speaks for the 600 million people of mainland China. We think the old excuse that we cannot recognize mainland China because it would mean accepting the concept of her sovereignty over Taiwan is not valid. We believe we can recognize the Chinese government on our own terms as being the government of mainland China, and the nationalist government as being the government of Formosa. We believe that China should be seated at the

United Nations, and that Canada's representatives in the United Nations should vote to have China so seated. There can be no nuclear disarmament or general disarmament as long as a country with 600 million people stays outside the community of nations. We cannot expect her to obey the laws of the community if we will not let her become a member of that community.
I want to repeat what I said to the Prime Minister yesterday in referring to a question, and say this. We trust the government will make no commitment to send Canadian troops to Cyprus unless those troops are under the aegis of the United Nations. We were glad to hear the Prime Minister make some statement on this point yesterday. We do not think Canada should get drawn into a power play between Great Britain, Cyprus, Turkey and Greece. If Canada is to take part in a peace keeping force then we think our troops should be there as the servants of the United Nations and not become embroiled in what could be a bitter and bloody family quarrel.
We in this group will insist that if the government is to sell uranium to France, as has been suggested in the press, it should have the necessary inspection service in order to be absolutely sure that such uranium is not used for military purposes. France is one of the few nations which have refused to sign the partial nuclear test ban agreement. Canada, which is a signatory, owes it to the other nations which are signatories to see that we do not sell uranium to any country, least of all to a country which has refused to sign a test ban agreement, unless we have the necessary facilities to make sure that the uranium is not finding its way into the hands of military forces.
I should like to tell the government that I think many people were disappointed that since parliament last met this country has acquired nuclear weapons in North Bay and La Macaza. As a matter of fact the nuclear warheads at La Macaza arrived, I understand, on New Year's eve, which I do not think was a good way to wish a happy new year to the Canadian people.
I do not intend to argue over again the trenchant case which I think can be made for Canada not becoming a nuclear power. I shall not take the time in which to do so on this occasion because the time available to me is fleeing. But I do wish to say that anything, whether nuclear arms or anything else, which ties us too closely to the United States in the present situation in the western hemisphere ought to make us pause and consider. There is the situation in Panama. There is the Cuban situation, in which a ridiculous embargo is being imposed on the people of Cuba because 20220-6i
The Address-Mr. Douglas the United States does not agree with their government. Only recently we heard of the farcical fishing episode in which 29 Cuban fishermen were thrown into a cell 20 feet by 25 feet in size, without bunks or chairs, and charged with an offence under a state ordinance of fishing without a licence. This was done in complete violation of international law. As one daily newspaper in this province said, when a gnat can stampede an elephant nobody is safe. We ought to be very careful that we do not tie ourselves to any program by which hysterical governments could precipitate this country into a war.
I wish to express the hope that the Prime Minister, although he accepted nuclear weapons because he thought the previous administration made a commitment-I do not think they did, but the Prime Minister is probably in possession of facts which I do not know anything about-but when he accepted those nuclear weapons he told the Canadian people he was prepared to negotiate this country out of them. I want to say to him now that should he decide to do this he will have the wholehearted support of the great majority of the Canadian people. We say to him "Start negotiating". Let us get rid of nuclear arms.
