speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am grateful to you and to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) for agreeing to delay the decision on the subamendment, thus permitting me to make my contribution at this time. First of all I would extend my congratulations to the mover and the seconder of the address in reply to the speech from the throne, to the hon. member for Longueuil (Mr. Cote) and the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard (Mr. Basford). I likewise would extend to the new ministers and the new parliamentary secretaries my congratulations upon being appointed to their new positions.
We listened with considerable interest this afternoon to the speech of the leader of the official opposition and to that of the Prime Minister. We realized as we listened to these capable contributions that we are again back in parliament, faced with the responsibilities we were elected to cope with as members of this house.
Briefly commenting on the speech from the throne, it certainly was not the statement of progress and reform that some of us had expected and particularly hoped for. There was little evidence of the Are, enthusiasm and dynamic courage that we heard so much about prior to the government assuming office. The promise of new paths has far too quickly turned into what is apparently a decision to go along with the status quo. When the first session of this parliament assembled we were stirringly promised a government that would lead us along new paths. We were promised 60 days of action. I do not think any of us then thought that those memorable 60 days would be the only days of action of this twenty sixth parliament. None of us
[Mr. Speaker.!
dreamed, I am sure, that within a matter of a few months this picture of challenging new adventures in the field of government would be no more charged with leadership than the speech from the throne that was delivered this week.
Looking at the throne speech constructively, there are some positive points which I think are worthy of mention, even though a number of them are carryovers from the last session. It is with some degree of satisfaction that we have seen that a new defence policy is taking shape. It is also encouraging to know that the defence committee will be enabled to continue its work this session, that a white paper on defence will be laid before this house before too long, and that at last we are to have a long term defence policy. I think this is urgently needed.
It is also interesting to note that there is new interest in the working conditions and welfare of Canada's work force. Much has been said today about the announcement that interest free loans will be available to those studying in our institutions of higher learning. When speaking this afternoon the Prime Minister mentioned that this was an innovation. I am not sure that it is; the province of Alberta for many years now has carried on this policy, as has the province of Saskatchewan. However, it is a commendable step. Certainly we must make our institutions of higher education available to those who show initiative and capability and wish to further their education in these institutions.
The government has spoken very firmly with regard to the Canada pension plan. While we understand that there is a tremendous need for a permanent, positive pension scheme for the Canadian people, we recognize that one of the most important aspects of this scheme is its portability. I hope the government will not move too hastily with the Canadian pension plan, because for it to be successful it is imperative that there should be the complete agreement and co-operation of the provincial governments.
A definite assurance has been given that legislation will be introduced into this house relating to the recommendations of the Mac-Pherson report with regard to transportation, and the O'Leary report with regard to the publications industry of this country. I was particularly pleased to hear the Prime Minister state in some detail this afternoon the situation relating to our publications. Just the other day I read a report which gives the loss in advertising revenue of seven of our major Canadian magazines during 1963. Two of them have since gone out of the publications business altogether. This report shows that there has been a drop since 1962 of

nearly $1,200,000 in advertising revenue alone. I would say to you, Mr. Prime Minister, that we will give our complete support to the program outlined this afternoon, because I think it is something that is long past due and should have been introduced a couple of years ago.
We are also interested in the fact that the ratification of the Columbia river treaty will be made possible in the near future. This is one project that can give a tremendous boost to the economy of this country, and top priority must be given to it and to the decision of the government to change the boundaries of our coastal waters as they relate to fisheries and our territorial waters.
The decision to extend farm credit is something that farmers across the country will welcome. The farm credit restrictions, as they were laid down ten years ago, no longer meet the needs of our farmers today simply because of the increased cost of farming operations at every level. This is something that is also very urgently required. I also say to you, Mr. Prime Minister, that we are pleased you have taken the lead in announcing this afternoon that procedural reforms are to be discussed and, I trust, decided favourably upon, by this house. Certainly there are many ways in which we can improve the functioning of parliament and make it more efficient and effective as we go about that work which we have before us from day to day. Again, we are more than pleased to give our full co-operation to any reasonable suggestions that are made along that line.
However, what does concern me is the government's conspicuous silence on many matters of great national importance. There was no mention of the Bank Act revision, which is supposed to take place this year according to the act itself. This afternoon the Minister of Finance recommended or suggested that there will be a recommendation that this revision be postponed for a year in order to permit the royal commission on banking and finance to submit its report. That is a good suggestion if it means that we will get down to some serious thinking, with the intention of bringing about some of the changes which ought to be made in the Bank Act.
No mention has been made of any permanent legislation relating to the extension of the municipal development and loan fund. Probably there is no government level in our country so urgently in need of capital funds as our local governments. The legislation introduced last year, while it had some effect for the immediate future, certainly was no long range solution to this problem. It is essential that our social capital needs be met
The Address-Mr. Thompson not by bringing in more capital from the outside at high expense, but by using our own Bank of Canada to provide the capital for the public segment of our economy.
No mention has been made of the Canada development fund which a great number of Canadians hoped would make possible a greater participation of Canadian capital in the development of our own resources and our own industry and commerce. Nothing has been said about the new fiscal and economic approaches which I am convinced are necessary if this old system of ours, which is showing itself so weak in so many places, is to continue to function. I am reminded of the story of the man who threw out a devil and cleaned up his house; but because he did not make provision for putting something else in its place seven worse devils came in to occupy the house. It is absolutely necessary that the problems we are facing in Canada today be met with realistic and dynamic and courageous solutions if we are to expect a change in a situation which has been limping along ever since the effect of the prosperity of world war II wore off about eight or nine years ago.
This government has done well to clean up some of the administrative confusion left by the previous administration, but now it must set a firm and definite direction for the country, particularly if its fiscal and budgetary policies let Canada's economy slip back to an even more difficult position than it was in in the past, and which we tend to neglect because we see that at the present we have a fairly prosperous year ahead of us. Positive and courageous action is necessary if Canada is to keep moving forward.
The motto that is hung before our eyes at the present time spells out in words of one syllable "Don't rock the boat". The cold war is said to be thawing. The economic situation seems to be improving. Action on our part is at least as likely to make matters worse or better. We should forget stout leadership and carry on housekeeping. I do not think that is good enough, even though in itself it is desirable. This humility on the part of the government is commendable; but it is a government that won an election campaign, or at least won a larger membership than any of the other parties, by criticizing the devaluation of the dollar and is now steadily maintaining that same policy. Where are the new paths? What are the new paths? Are there any new paths? This nation would like to know.
Canadians look to this parliament to give the leadership which will reaffirm our own stability and solidarity, both politically and economically. Our responsibilities begin for each of us here in this house. As members of

The Address-Mr. Thompson the opposition and of the government in a house of minorities there is a peculiar responsibility placed on each one of us which is not so evident or perhaps so needful in the case of a large majority. It is in this particular situation that all of us carry a load of responsibility to the people of Canada whom we represent.
All of this adds up to the simple fact, which I think each one of us admits, that Canada is at the crossroads. We have just three years left before our centennial, and in those three years there is a great deal that must be done if our centennial is going to be worth celebrating. We must ask ourselves, what is Canada? What do we want Canada to be? It has been said that Canada is a nation without a purpose, full of quarrelling and disunity. If this is so, then we must have faith in our future before we can take the right action today.
Therefore I think this parliament's top priority must be predominantly domestic, simply because our most important problems are right here. Too often we speak in negatives. We are happy we are not Americans; we are equally happy we are not British; but too seldom we are nothing in our negative approach. I am concerned because we do not have any real awareness of nationalistic feelings. Some tell us that Canada needs a rebirth of that spirit which existed 100 years ago; that we must return to the partnership which originated confederation. But I ask this house and every Canadian, what is that spirit?
If we go back and study the debates which took place at the Quebec conferences of 1864, and refer to the discussions and debates which continued through to confederation in 1867, we will find that there were two basic purposes behind the discussions of the fathers of confederation. One was simply that there was going to be a nation called Canada, independent of the United States, independent ultimately of any colonial connection with the mother countries across the Atlantic. The American civil war was just in its final stages, and there was the fear that this tremendous military might which was represented in the victorious part of the United States would look northward and want to take in Canada. So they wanted to be a country. This is something we want to be today much more than we are speaking or even thinking about.
The second predominant thought, it seemed to me on reading through those debates, that record of what was the thinking of those fathers of confederation, was that they wanted to give a guarantee to the minorities, whoever they were and wherever they were to be found. This is something which today, is underneath the disunity and unrest which
[Mr. Thompson.!
exists in our nation, simply because too many are afraid of those rights and privileges which we regard as essential in a democracy to a minority. What is necessary for us to do is to come back to basic essentials. We must establish a horizontal base across our nation on which our provinces can rest. There is no sense in talking about provincial autonomy unless there is a sense of national responsibility first, unless there is across the country a solid foundation to make Canada a nation, then any vertical divisions into which we might cut ourselves will amount to nothing at all.
I believe the question can be summed up briefly by saying that we need a new awareness of national responsibility and a new guarantee of provincial autonomy; that we need not just platitudes but action. There has been too much talk. What we need now is something which will prove that we mean what our words have said.
I submit that legislation alone will never bring this about. The scriptures say "The letter killeth but the spirit giveth life". That is something which was very real and evident to the fathers of confederation. Perhaps one of those who 100 years ago understood this best was Hon. George Brown. He was a man of strong religious convictions who did not pretend to understand those with whom he willingly entered into confederation. With a spirit of vision he said:
Our scheme is to establish a government which will seek to turn the tide of European emigration into this northern half of the American continent -which will strive to develop its great natural resources-and which will endeavour to maintain liberty, and justice, and Christianity throughout the land.
Yes, facing facts realistically one might say it is true things are not so bad. The F.L.Q. is less active than it was. Nobody has dynamited any bridges or armouries of late. On the other hand, enough firearms and ammunition have been stolen in well planned armoury raids in the last few weeks to enable some people to cause a great deal of trouble at an appropriate time.
I do not think, however, that the long term future of the province of Quebec or any province has come any nearer to a solution. Rather I feel that there has been a hardening of attitudes in Quebec and in other parts of Canada as well. Therefore the time has come when by action we should lay down what is the responsible attitude to the nation at large, and a guarantee at the same time to the provinces of the autonomy which they regard and respect.
The Prime Minister has talked eloquently tonight about what is necessary in Canada at this time. If these are the sentiments of

the government then I think we can all agree with them. But they carry with them the responsibility to put those sentiments into actual effect and practice. We are troubled, we say, because Canada seems to be a country without unity. Yet how can men be united except they have some common purpose to hold them together? How can we plan lor the future and invest and work today to make those plans come true unless we know the sort of future that we, the Canadian people, are planning for ourselves through our elected representatives in parliament?
It is time that we as a nation realized the simple economic power of a strong desire to be a nation that knows what it wants. The communist nations of the world know well enough what they want. Year after year for the past 20 years, if not longer, we have seen them slowly and steadily achieving their aims, creeping like an evil fungus across the globe. We knew it in wartime. At the first outbreak of hostilities Canada's unemployment began to disappear like magic. Our factories, our mines and our people started working together as never before. Provincial and federal governments worked together in a common cause against a common enemy.
Why can we not fight like that in peacetime for those things that we say we believe in? If we would take an idea like this to heart we could make Canada's centennial a year of rejoicing across the whole globe.
As we look from this base, Canada, at the world we can understand that the world also is in turmoil. The prime minister of the United Kingdom during his visit a few days ago said that he thought the cold war was over, and that we should now be trying to convince the communist countries to cease their subversive activities and local wars. I say it would take a well trained ostrich to be really hopeful for a world in which the President of the United States was assassinated by a self confessed Marxist on November 22 last, and in which revolutions and disturbances against established forms of government taking place every week since then in Panama, Viet Nam and Cyprus in the northern hemisphere and along a strategic line across Africa around the 10th parallel of latitude south of the equator in Zanzibar, Tanganyika, Ruanda, the Congo and Gabon, all in a short period of less than two months.
Thus we do have a responsibility abroad as well. It was good to hear the leader of the official opposition and the Prime Minister refer to the commonwealth. It seems that all too often the commonwealth is something that we relegate to the upstairs attic. I am convinced that if we really want to make the commonwealth work as a team it could be
The Address-Mr. Thompson much an influence for good today in the world such as the British empire was 50 or 100 years ago. But we have to do something to convince ourselves of that. It is interesting to note that we are going to have a commonwealth conference here in Canada this summer. I think it might be a good suggestion to make to the Prime Minister that, as far as Canada is concerned, he make participation in the commonwealth conference completely non-partisan by bringing all parties into the discussions, so that we may come back to the realization that the commonwealth has yet a very important part to play.
I think we should be very careful about judging our country's welfare all the time simply by reference to abstract statistics such as the rate of economic growth. Economics can be a very good servant for men, but it can also be a very bad master. Our frenzied pursuit of a higher and higher gross national product is really nothing less than a glorification of more and more human effort, quite apart from whether that effort is well or badly directed, whether it is useful or whether it is just the effort of two men tugging at opposite ends of a rope in a tug of war.
We tend to worship statistics today when we should be thinking about people. We should be thinking about people at home and abroad; and when we do think about them, their daily worries, their debts, their incomes, their jobs, their need for more food, better clothing and better housing. I think we are at last forced to shake off our complacency. We are a rich country with more food than we know what to do with, a vast construction industry working well below capacity, and a textile industry not working full time while keeping our foreign clothing import quota. Yet at the same time some 40 per cent of our Canadan people are living below the poverty line in actual need of better food, better clothing and better shelter. Is this the climate in which we are letting complacency prevail?
The burning question today so far as our economy is concerned is summed up in the problem of automation. Here is a tool that can bring man wealth beyond him dreams, and all we do is worry about what it does in taking away employment. We shackle automation to try to make it conform to an economic system of the horse and buggy age. This cannot go on forever. Automation is too strong for it.
The mistake of our economic system today, one mistake at any rate, is that although production comes from a combination of land, labour and capital, and in this combination labour is going to become progressively less important, we still expect 95 per cent of our population to gain their living from nothing else than the sale of their labour. To do this

The Address-Mr. Thompson even up to the present point has led to terrible distortions in our economic system. We build houses at the worst time of the winter to maintain employment. We try to move industries to uneconomic locations, again to keep up employment. I am waiting for the day when it is moved in this house to authorize the federal government to pay farmers a special subsidy of $50 a ton on potatoes provided they are grown between the months of November and March. It might certainly keep up employment for the farmers.
I say this not because I lack sympathy in any way for the unemployed. I say it because we are attempting to bend our economic system in an entirely impossible direction. Sooner or later we are going to reach the breaking point.
I just have a few more remarks to make, Mr. Speaker, and I wonder whether the house would grant me the privilege of continuing.

speechtext:
Thank you. What we
should be doing is taking a long, hard look at the ownership of land and the ownership of capital in this country. We should be finding out who is receiving the unearned income from these sources. We should be seeing that the average man in the street is receiving a fair income not only from his labour but from his nation's capital and its natural resources. This is what the Social Credit provincial governments of this country are striving to do as much as is within their power, and I commend them for it. This is what the national government of Canada should be striving to do as well.
I think we have to face up to the fact that the economic system we inherited from our forefathers is at the point of breaking down. It came to us from an age of scarcity. We live in an age of abundance. The economic question of our time is, by what means is this abundance to be distributed? Our present system certainly is not doing it satisfactorily.
There are two possible answers. There is the one toward which we are actually drifting in this country at the present time. It is the answer that the state starts distributing all needed services to the citizens free, that is by taking away a progressively greater share of income by taxation. In the end the man in the street finds that the state takes everything and provides everything in the form of free services, that is soup kitchens, medical plans and handouts in every shape and form. In effect this is to abandon the money system altogether, and so abandon one of the finest instruments mankind has


ever devised for obtaining individual and personal satisfaction of his wants, no matter what they may be.
The other choice, and it is the one our party favours, is to adapt our financial system to work in this new age of plenty that is upon us. There is no middle ground to tread between these different policies, and I make no bones about expecting them to form the dividing line of the two party system in this parliament some time in the future. The question is, are we to master the economic machine we have created or let it master us? Are we to bask in the sunshine of economic prosperity or button our coats to economic adversity, as if economic trends were as uncontrollable as the weather? If we do we are making a big mistake, because the workings of our economic system obey understandable rules. Man has made the system, and man can control it if he has the will.
It is a question of will, because many in this country do not have the will to see things changed. They sit at the top of the heap and cannot see the misery underneath. They hold the reins of financial power over governments and citizens alike and see no reason for change. When we reflect on the economic miracles that can take place so easily in wartime, is it not time we caught a vision of what a genuine war to end want on a world scale would really be like? Is it not time we caught a vision of Canadian task forces in all parts of the globe bringing techniques of the twentieth century to nations that are now underprivileged and in want? I do not believe we realize in the least the power for good that Canada could be in this world at the present time. It is not so much a matter of immense expenditures as of having the right men available with the right ideas at the right times. With the right amount of organization and good will we could make Canada's centennial year a blessing to the whole world and set back the advancement of communism a thousand years.
We meet here once again in parliament with a minority government. I believe that this, too, places a clear choice upon us as members of the House of Commons. We are a representative cross-section of the Canadian people at the present time, with all the conflicts of interest, special concerns and differences of policy that characterize the Canadian people outside this chamber. One choice we have is to determinedly learn to carry out the task our country has sent us here to do, that is to act as advisers to Her Majesty in carrying on the government of this country. Our other choice is to confess our unwillingness or our inability to do this, and ask the nation once again to replace us.

It remains my firm belief that this minority parliament can provide good government for Canada, better government in fact than is being achieved at this time or than would be achieved by an over-all majority. In the complex task of deciding on our nation's future, I believe it is providential that we are in a situation where every voice must be heard and considered and where the views of the minority cannot be swept aside.
I believe that the immense strides forward that have been taken in this house during the past year toward meeting and mastering the problems of defence are only an indication of what can be achieved when members meet, not as politicians but as Canadians in a serious endeavour to understand the problems and do what is best for their country. I hope it will be possible to extend this spirit of constructive, forward thinking into other fields during the coming year. Let us achieve this, avoiding unnecessary partisanship and this may yet prove to be one of the finest parliaments Canada has ever had.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: I wonder if before you leave the chair, Mr. Speaker, we might not recognize the new house leader, who is alleged to be completely non-partisan and who is reputed to be a non-controversial figure. Does the government intend to carry on this debate on the address to its completion without interruption?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Now that I am in order, Mr. Speaker, I will say yes, the government intends to carry on tomorrow with the leaders' speeches and then with the debate on the address.
